title: Complications of Paediatric Diabetes
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Paediatric diabetes complications encompass life-threatening acute metabolic crises like diabetic ketoacidosis and cerebral oedema, alongside progressive microvascular and macrovascular damage. Early identification hinges on clinical suspicion in resource-limited settings.

sections.p: Paediatric diabetes complications are categorized into acute emergencies and chronic tissue damage. Acute diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is defined biochemically by blood glucose >11 mmol/L, venous pH <7.3 or serum bicarbonate <15 mmol/L, and significant ketonaemia or ketonuria.
b: Acute metabolic crises: DKA and severe hypoglycaemia
Chronic microvascular disease: retinopathy, nephropathy, and peripheral neuropathy
Chronic macrovascular disease: accelerated atherosclerosis and peripheral vascular disease
Renal papillary necrosis and soft-tissue gangrene occur with longstanding disease

sections.p: DKA severity is classified by the degree of acidosis rather than the blood glucose level.
b: Mild DKA: venous pH 7.2 to <7.3, or bicarbonate 10 to <15 mmol/L
Moderate DKA: venous pH 7.1 to <7.2, or bicarbonate 5 to <10 mmol/L
Severe DKA: venous pH <7.1, or bicarbonate <5 mmol/L
Chronic microvascular staging: microalbuminuria precedes persistent proteinuria; non-proliferative retinopathy precedes proliferative disease

sections.p: Acute complications in children are usually precipitated by infection or missed insulin doses. Chronic complications stem from cumulative tissue exposure to chronic hyperglycaemia.
b: Infections: severe malaria, pneumonia, gastroenteritis, urinary tract infections, tuberculosis
Non-adherence: unaffordable insulin, lack of cold-chain storage, syringe shortages
First presentation: previously undiagnosed Type 1 diabetes presenting directly in DKA
Traditional treatments: stopping insulin to use herbal remedies or faith-healing alternatives
Chronic complications: prolonged high HbA1c driving microvascular and macrovascular basement-membrane thickening

sections.p: Children present along a spectrum from subacute polyuria to deep coma with respiratory compensation.
b: Polyuria, polydipsia, and marked weight loss over weeks
Kussmaul breathing: deep, rapid, unlaboured hyperventilation to blow off carbon dioxide
Abdominal pain and recurrent vomiting mimicking an acute surgical abdomen
Dehydration signs: sunken eyes, dry tongue, delayed capillary refill, and weak pulses
Altered sensorium: irritability, lethargy, or coma indicating severe DKA or cerebral oedema
Hypoglycaemia: sweating, tremors, hunger, and seizures during overtreatment or missed meals

t.b: Detects hyperglycaemia (>11 mmol/L in DKA) or life-threatening hypoglycaemia
Confirms ketonuria and glycosuria at bedside when blood testing is unavailable
Determines acidosis severity (pH <7.3, bicarbonate <15 mmol/L) to stage DKA
Identifies hypokalaemia or pseudohyponatraemia to guide safe potassium replacement

t.a: Malaria rapid test and blood film
t.b: Rule out endemic co-infection triggering metabolic decompensation
Detects urinary tract infection, pyuria, or shedding seen in papillary necrosis
Screens for early diabetic nephropathy after puberty or 5 years of disease duration
Screens for early diabetic retinopathy, microaneurysms, and prevents blindness

sections.p: The most catastrophic acute complication is cerebral oedema, often caused by rapid fluid shifts or early insulin boluses.
b: Cerebral oedema: headache, bradycardia, rising blood pressure, vomiting, dropping GCS
Refractory hypokalaemia causing fatal cardiac arrhythmias during insulin infusions
Hypoglycaemia from excessive insulin or delayed dextrose infusion
Aspiration pneumonia in children with depressed consciousness and vomiting
Renal papillary necrosis presenting with flank pain, macroscopic haematuria, and renal impairment
Soft-tissue gangrene due to peripheral vascular compromise

sections.p: Treatment requires structured resuscitation, gradual rehydration, delayed insulin administration, and potassium replacement to prevent cerebral oedema and cardiac arrest.
b: Resuscitation: normal saline 0.9% fluid bolus over 1 hour only if shocked
Rehydration: calculate deficit and maintenance; replace evenly over 48 hours to avoid brain swelling
Insulin: start soluble regular insulin infusion after initial fluid resuscitation, never give IV boluses
Potassium: add potassium chloride to IV fluids once urine output is confirmed, unless hyperkalaemic
Add 5% dextrose once blood glucose drops to prevent precipitous osmolality drops
Treat triggers: broad-spectrum antibiotics for sepsis or antimalarials for malaria; avoid empiric sodium bicarbonate

sections.p: Prevention requires continuous patient education, reliable medicine access, and regular screening for microvascular disease.
b: Monitor blood glucose and urine ketones regularly at local clinics
Ensure home insulin cold-chain using clay pots filled with wet sand in rural homes
Annual screening from age 11 years (or 2-5 years post-diagnosis) for retinopathy and nephropathy
Education on sick-day rules: never omit insulin during acute febrile illnesses
Screen for co-existing autoimmune conditions like coeliac disease and hypothyroidism
Severe pneumonia: Kussmaul breathing has clear chest sounds unlike pneumonia-related tachypnoea
Acute appendicitis: DKA causes ketotic abdominal pain and vomiting with high glucose
Cerebral malaria: both present with coma; check blood film, glucose, and urine ketones
Severe dehydration from gastroenteritis: marked polyuria occurs despite profound fluid loss
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: extreme glucose, severe dehydration, but minimal acidosis and ketosis
Serum sodium: falsely low due to osmotic fluid shifts (pseudohyponatraemia)
Serum potassium: appears normal or elevated in blood despite severe total-body potassium deficit
Leukocyte count: leukocytosis is common in DKA from stress demargination, not necessarily infection
Urine ketones: dipsticks measure acetoacetate, missing beta-hydroxybutyrate during early recovery
Haemoglobinopathies: sickle cell disease or severe malaria can falsely alter HbA1c readings

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent vomiting or inability to tolerate oral fluids
Deep, rapid breathing or breath smelling of acetone
Sudden worsening headache, lethargy, or confusion
Blood glucose repeatedly reading high despite insulin administration

faq.q: Why is an IV insulin bolus contraindicated in paediatric DKA?
faq.a: IV insulin boluses cause a precipitous drop in intravascular osmolality, dramatically increasing the risk of fatal cerebral oedema and sudden hypokalaemia.

faq.q: How can families keep insulin cool without electricity?
faq.a: Evaporative cooling using a clay pot filled with damp sand or wrapping vials in wet cloth keeps insulin viable in warm climates.

faq.q: Why is bicarbonate therapy avoided in DKA?
faq.a: Bicarbonate causes paradoxical central nervous system acidosis, worsens hypokalaemia, and increases the incidence of cerebral oedema.

exam: A child with DKA suddenly develops headache, bradycardia, and rising blood pressure. What is the diagnosis and immediate management? — Suspect cerebral oedema; elevate the head of the bed, reduce fluid rates, and immediately administer IV hypertonic saline or mannitol before waiting for imaging.

Why must potassium be added to maintenance fluids even if baseline serum potassium is normal? — Insulin drives potassium into cells and acidosis resolution shifts potassium intracellularly, causing catastrophic hypokalaemia if not replenished.

A 7-year-old presents with deep, rapid breathing and clear chest auscultation. What is the clinical sign and significance? — Kussmaul breathing; it represents respiratory compensation for severe metabolic acidosis, classic for DKA.

How do you distinguish DKA abdominal pain from an acute surgical abdomen? — DKA pain resolves within hours of fluid and insulin therapy; surgical causes persist and lack severe metabolic acidosis or ketonuria.

Why is 5% dextrose added to IV fluids when glucose drops to around 14 to 17 mmol/L? — To prevent hypoglycaemia and allow continuous insulin infusion to clear ketoacids while avoiding rapid osmolality changes.

Why is total-body potassium depleted despite normal initial serum potassium in DKA? — Osmotic diuresis causes severe urinary potassium wasting, but acidosis shifts potassium out of cells into serum, masking the deficit.
